issues.issue: The recital defines "Premises" to include "all rights, privileges and easements ... and all related and future improvements", a catch-all whose outer boundary is undefined against the enumerated parking, entrances, exits and access routes.

The recital states the Building is approximately 47,450 square feet while operative Section 1.2 fixes the Rentable Area at the numeral "(47,480)" square feet, so recital and operative text point to different areas on which Base Rent is based.

"Main level" floor area measured "from the outside of the exterior walls and the center line of any common (or party) walls" gives no rule for mezzanine-level or partially enclosed areas beyond the express exclusions.
The written words "forty-seven thousand, four hundred fifty" contradict the parenthetical numeral "(47,480)", a mechanical error in the very figure on which Base Rent is expressly based.
The stated Rentable Area also differs from the approximately 47,450 square feet recited in the Recitals, leaving the two statements of the same measurement inconsistent.

A flat "fifteen (15) years" sits against Section 2.2 (expiry on the last day of the fifteenth Lease Year, itself measured from the first day of the first full month) and Section 3.3's automatic extension to January 31, so the actual initial term can exceed fifteen years.

The definition offers two alternative start points ("beginning with the Commencement Date, or the first day of the first full month") without saying which controls, leaving a gap period between the Commencement Date and the first full month unallocated to any Lease Year.

The no-default condition on renewal cannot be squared with Section 3.2, under which the options "shall be automatically exercised with no action required by Tenant"; it is unclear whether a default at the automatic-exercise date defeats a renewal that has already occurred.
"the Rent shall be as adjusted sel forth in Section 4" is grammatically broken, leaving unclear whether only Base Rent or all components of Rent are adjusted on renewal.
Automatic exercise "with no action required by Tenant" sits against the opening words of Section 3, which condition the renewal option on Tenant not being in default.

The one-year notice to decline the January 31 extension is keyed to "the expiration of the initial or renewal term then in effect", which is itself the date the extension would move, making the notice deadline self-referential.

Rent payable "without deduction or setoff for any reason whatsoever" contradicts Section 17.2(b), which expressly lets Tenant abate Base Rent, Percentage Rent and Additional Rent, and Section 4.5's Base Rent Credit.
The rent table's year ranges are internally garbled ("4-5" and "41-75" for the initial fifteen-year term), so the years to which each per-square-foot rate applies cannot be read off the table.

"an assignment or subleasing for a use other than a retail use such that Percentage Rent would not be applicable" gives no test for what is a "retail use", and the formula produces no increase at all if no Percentage Rent was owed in the prior five Lease Years.

The premise that on a Non-retail Transfer "Percentage Rent would not be applicable" cannot be squared with Section 4.2, which prescribes a prorated Percentage Rent Threshold "in the event of a Non-retail Transfer".

The twelve Allocated Thresholds total $1,300,000, one tenth of the $13,000,000 Percentage Rent Threshold they are said to allocate, a mechanical error that changes the rent payable in any partial Lease Year.

Exclusion (i) ends with the general phrase "and other receipts which are remitted to a governmental or other licensing entity", whose reach against the enumerated hunting and fishing licence receipts is uncertain.

The acknowledgment that Tenant "has no obligation to operate for the Specific Permitted Use ... or any other business" sits against Section 8.2's affirmative requirement that Tenant open a Gander Mountain store within one year of the Delivery Date and Landlord's recapture right on cessation.

Defining Additional Rent as "all amounts required to be paid by Tenant under the terms of this Lease" leaves it uncertain whether damages, indemnity payments and Base Rent itself become Additional Rent.

The clause fixes a $8,050 Monthly Credit "in each Lease Year (until the Base Rent Credit is applied in full)" but does not say what happens if the certified spend is less than $675,000, leaving the number of monthly credits to be inferred.

Acceptance of the Building "in its 'as is' condition, with all faults and defects ... without representation or warranty" contradicts Section 24.1's representation that the Premises comply with all existing laws and Section 23.2's environmental representations.

"in a manner consistent with a Gander Mountain prototype building" is an undefined external standard, and Landlord's approval right is limited to components which "adversely affect the structural integrity" without a measure of adverse effect.

Tenant's exclusive right to "the pylon sign on the Land (as may be identified on Exhibit B)" depends on Exhibit B, which in this instrument is an unexecuted placeholder listing only what it is "[t]o show".

The definition sweeps in "all real estate taxes and assessments which may at any time be imposed in lieu of, in addition to or in substitution of same", a catch-all whose reach beyond the enumerated real estate taxes and assessments is uncertain.

The exclusion runs from enumerated gift, franchise, estate and transfer taxes to "any other tax, assessment, charge or levy upon the Rent", and is then partly taken back by a substitute-tax proviso, leaving the boundary between excluded and payable taxes contestable.

Tenant waives any right to cancel or seek diminution of Rent "unless such right is explicitly reserved to Tenant under the terms of this Lease", and what counts as an explicit reservation is left unstated.

The deemed certification that the Premises and parking area "have been completed in accordance with the requirements and terms of this Lease" is difficult to reconcile with Section 26.5's Access Conversion and parking-ratio conditions and Section 17.2's abatement remedy.

The Premises may be used for "any lawful purpose" including firearms sales, yet the same section bars use as "a shooting gallery", a term left undefined and hard to square with in-store firearms demonstration.

Section 23.3 has Landlord acknowledge that Tenant's contemplated use involves the "display, sale and demonstration of firearms, smokeless powder, black powder [and] ammunition", which sits uneasily with this section's prohibition on a shooting gallery.

The mandatory opening obligation in the first sentence sits against the section heading and the disclaimer in Section 4.2 that Tenant "has made no covenant to continuously operate" and has no obligation to operate any business on the Premises.
Landlord's recapture notice need only be given "following the expiration of such nine (9) month period", with no outside date, so how long the right survives a cessation is left open.

Permitted promotional activities "may include, but are not limited to" boat display and duck calling events, so the outer limit of permitted outside activity is set only by the open-ended reference to the Specific Permitted Use.

The covenant operates only "[f]or so long as the Premises are used for the Specific Excluded Use", a term defined later in the same sentence as the competing use of other property, and the 5% qualifier's "its retail sales" has no clear antecedent.

Conditioning the covenant on the Premises being used for the Specific Excluded Use cannot readily be squared with Section 8.2, under which Tenant may cease operating entirely in its sole discretion, so the restriction could evaporate at Tenant's election.

The express grant of damages for breach of Section 9.1 is in tension with Exhibit D, Section 3, in which the Restricted Party acknowledges "that damages are not adequate" for enforcement of the same restriction.

The carve-out for replacements when "less than three (3) years remain in the term" does not say whether the term includes the renewal terms, which under Section 3.2 are automatically exercised unless Tenant gives notice.

It is unclear how the $5,000,000 Base Coverage Requirement "when combined with umbrella insurance" relates to the separate $25,000,000 excess layer, and the self-insurance proviso is left grammatically unclosed.

The section requires Tenant to insure the personal property only "to at least eighty percent (80%)" of replacement value but "all buildings and improvements" to full replacement value, and never says who is named insured or loss payee of the building coverage.

Who is entitled to the building proceeds is left to Section 15.2 (escrow disbursed to Tenant as restoration progresses) and Section 15.4 (proceeds assigned to Landlord on a late-term termination), which pull in different directions on the same coverage.

Section 13.1.1 makes Tenant indemnify for any injury "occurring in, on, or about the Premises" while carving out only Landlord's gross negligence or willful misconduct, so whether Tenant must indemnify Landlord against Landlord's own ordinary negligence is genuinely contestable.

The gross-negligence carve-out is itself undone by the words "unless Tenant is compensated therefor by insurance", which sits awkwardly with Section 12.1's requirement that Landlord be named an additional insured on Tenant's liability policy.

Landlord indemnifies only for its "gross negligence or willful misconduct", a term the Lease nowhere defines, and the carve-out for Tenant's ordinary negligence makes the two indemnities overlap in the same event.

Landlord's approval right extends only to a component which "adversely affects the structural integrity of the Building", with no threshold of adversity, and the residual permission is qualified by the vague words "except as provided for in this Lease".

The obligation "to otherwise secure the Landlord to its satisfaction promptly upon request" sets a purely subjective standard with no reasonableness qualifier, and "first class, workmanlike manner" is undefined.

Tenant's unconditional duty to repair and restore after any casualty must be read against Section 15.4, which relieves Tenant of any restoration obligation if it terminates, and Section 16.2, which puts restoration after a partial taking on Landlord.

The escrow mechanism assumes proceeds of Tenant's policy will fund restoration, which has to be reconciled with Section 12.2's permission for Tenant to satisfy the building coverage "through Tenant's self-insurance" and with Section 15.4's assignment of proceeds to Landlord.

The flat statement that no damage "shall entitle or permit Tenant to surrender or terminate this Lease" contradicts Section 15.4, which expressly permits Tenant to terminate after late-term damage, and Section 16.2's rent abatement during restoration.

"Tenant may terminate this Lease by giving written notice to the other" leaves the notice recipient unnamed, a drafting slip left over from a mutual right, and condition (a) is triggered by any repair taking more than sixty days.

Rent is to be "equitably adjusted" on termination and "equitably apportioned according to the floor space so taken" if the Lease continues, with no formula or decision-maker identified for either adjustment.

After listing loss of business, depreciation, removal of stock and relocation expenses, the proviso ends with "or any other damages allowed Tenant by law", leaving unclear how much of the award reserved to Landlord that catch-all takes back.
"Accelerate" is not defined, and the sentence does not say whether it bars only a demand for the discounted present value of the remaining term or also a judgment for future rent as it falls due.

The bar on acceleration sits directly against the earlier sentences of Section 17.1, which preserve "Tenant's liability for ... future rent and other charges to accrue hereunder" and allow Landlord to recover "all other damages reasonably sustained" after re-entry.

The section's structure is broken: a clause "(b) Landlord defaults in the performance of the covenant of quiet possession" appears with no preceding "(a)", and a second lettered pair (a)/(b) is then used for remedies, so the trigger for the five-day cure period is unclear.

Tenant's right to "abate the Base Rent, Percentage Rent and Additional Rent" contradicts Section 4's requirement that Rent be paid "without deduction or setoff for any reason whatsoever" and Section 7's waiver of any diminution of Rent.

A cumulative-remedies clause allowing any remedy "allowed by law" has to be read against Section 17.1's express bar on Landlord accelerating rent and Section 7's waiver of Tenant's termination remedies.

"The base rate of interest ... established in the Wall Street Journal" describes a rate the Journal reports rather than establishes, so the reference point for interest under Sections 17.2, 17.5 and 17.7 is imprecise.
After six specific certifications the clause requires "[a]ny other information reasonably requested", an open-ended catch-all whose reach against the enumerated items is uncertain.

The promise that Tenant need not sign anything "that differs materially from the attached form" has to be squared with Exhibit E's own terms, notably its Section 4, which overrides Tenant's Lease cancellation rights "[n]otwithstanding any provisions of the Lease to the contrary".

The promise that "Landlord shall remain fully liable on this Lease" for pre-transfer matters is contradicted by the immediately following paragraph, which frees the named Landlord of all obligations and states there shall be "no personal (or entity) liability of Landlord".

Within the paragraph the words "[t]here shall be no personal (or entity) liability of Landlord" sit against the immediately preceding sentence deeming each successor landlord to have "expressly assumed all obligations" of its predecessors.

The release of the named Landlord and the exculpation limiting Tenant to the Landlord's interest in the Premises contradict the preceding paragraph of Section 18.3, under which Landlord "shall remain fully liable on this Lease" for pre-transfer defaults.

Tenant's "absolute right ... without Landlord's further approval" is immediately qualified by the requirement that lender documents be "in a form acceptable to Landlord and Landlord's counsel", which restores the approval the first sentence removes.

The flat warranty of fee ownership sits against Section 18.3, which defines "Landlord" to include the owner of a leasehold interest under a ground lease, and Section 18.2, which contemplates a ground lessor of the Premises.

The representation is given "[a]s of the Commencement Date" although Section 19 introduces it as a present representation, and it depends on Exhibit G, which Section 25.11 elsewhere calls the Memorandum of Lease form.

The exception for "casualty damage (if it is Landlord's obligation ...) or casualty damage and damage resulting from eminent domain" repeats casualty damage on inconsistent conditions, obscuring what Tenant must repair on surrender.

The carve-out for "repairs which are Landlord's responsibility pursuant to its indemnification obligations under Section 13" mis-cites Section 13, which is an indemnity and imposes no repair obligation; repair responsibility is allocated by Section 11.

The definition reaches all requirements "otherwise relating to the environment or solid, liquid or hazardous substances" before a non-exclusive list of named statutes, leaving the catch-all's reach beyond the enumerated Acts uncertain.

"Hazardous Material" extends to anything regulated as hazardous, toxic "or under any other similar designation", a catch-all that on its face captures the black powder and petroleum products Tenant sells in the ordinary course.

The breadth of the definition has to be reconciled with Section 23.3, in which Landlord agrees Tenant's firearms, powder and camping-fuel sales do not violate the hazardous materials covenants, and with Section 23.6's carve-out for materials Tenant sells.

The first sentence gives an unqualified representation that Landlord has provided "full, accurate and complete copies" of all reports in its possession, while every following representation is limited to knowledge "without any independent inquiry or investigation".

Landlord's acknowledgment that Tenant's firearms, powder and petroleum-product sales do not violate this Section has to be reconciled with the same Section's strict prohibition on any Tenant Indemnified Person storing Hazardous Material except in strict compliance with Environmental Laws.

The exclusion for material "introduced onto the Premises by any Tenant Indemnified Person, or placed inside the four walls of the Building or on, in or under the Premises by an invitee or customer" is syntactically ambiguous as to whether the four-walls limit qualifies both branches.

The requirement that Tenant remediate only "after Landlord approval" has no reasonableness or time limit, and the closing sentence refers to any "clean up or rededication" of the Premises, a word with no meaning in context.

The representation that the Premises comply with all existing laws contradicts Section 5.1, under which Tenant accepts the Building "in its 'as is' condition, with all faults and defects ... without representation or warranty".

The proviso allocating the cost of required structural changes is garbled and partly illegible ("in | t such laws ... ind ubnot fo, the erection of a fire escape or exit, the same shall be complied with by L ole cost"), so who bears that cost cannot be read from the text.
The rule that the Lease prevails over any exhibit is hard to square with Exhibit E, Section 4, which by its terms overrides the Lease "[n]otwithstanding any provisions of the Lease to the contrary".

The excuse covers circumstances "beyond the Landlord's control, including, without limitation, labor disputes, embargoes, governmental restrictions ... acts of Tenant, war or other strife", so the reach of the general words beyond the listed events is undefined.

The clause calls for the Memorandum of Lease "in the form attached as Exhibit G", but Section 29 lists Exhibit F as the Memorandum of Lease and Exhibit G as Permitted Encumbrances, the exhibit relied on by Section 19.3.

The general reasonableness standard is qualified only by "[e]xcept as expressly provided otherwise", which must be reconciled with Sections 5.4 and 8.1, where Tenant may withhold consent "in its sole and absolute discretion".

A holdover tenancy "upon the same terms and conditions as herein provided" at 200% Base Rent has to be squared with Section 3.3, under which the term is automatically extended to the following January 31 unless Tenant gives notice.

The disclaimer that neither party is the scrivener sits against the notation on the attached Memorandum of Lease and Declaration of Restrictions that "[t]his instrument was drafted by: Gander Mountain Company Legal Department".

"[T]hen Tenant only may, in its sole election, terminate this Lease" is awkwardly worded, leaving it arguable whether the conditions lapse if not invoked by the Contingency Date and whether termination is the exclusive consequence.

The condition that all blanks and "incomplete exhibits" be completed cannot be squared with the instrument as executed, in which Exhibit B (the site plan relied on by Sections 5.4 and 8.4) remains a bracketed placeholder.

Satisfaction "shall require at a minimum, but shall not be limited to" the Access Conversion and a 4.2 parking ratio, so the enumerated minima do not fix what else Tenant may demand under the heading of adequate access and parking.

"[M]aterial adverse change" is left undefined and the list is internally garbled, referring to "the environmental condition of the Premises or the Premises" and then again to "the condition of the Building and the Premises".

The undertaking to "use reasonable efforts and diligence to enforce all of the provisions" of third-party agreements sets no benchmark, and the covenant reaches "any agreements with respect to the Premises" of unbounded scope.

The metes-and-bounds description contains an incomplete call ("to a point at its intersection with the division on the west and the property now or formerly owned by said Louis Tokos"), so one boundary line cannot be run from the text.

The form fixes the Expiration Date in 2019, which assumes fifteen years from a 2004 Commencement Date, while Section 2.2 measures expiry from the last day of the fifteenth Lease Year as defined in Section 2.4.

The recital says "Landlord owns" the Restricted Property, while the operative Sections 1 and 4 bind the "Restricted Party" — described in Recital B as an affiliate of Landlord — as the owner of that property.

The recital describes the Restricted Party simply as "an affiliate of Landlord", narrower than Section 9.1's definition of Restricted Parties, which reaches entities controlled by or affiliated with another entity affiliated with Landlord.

The restriction applies "[f]or so long as the Premises are used for the Specific Excluded Use", a term defined at the end of the same sentence as the competing use of the Restricted Property, and "its retail sales" in the 5% qualifier has no identified antecedent.

The list of restricted uses omits "sale of other casual apparel", which Section 9.1 of the Lease includes in the same Specific Excluded Use definition, so the recorded restriction is narrower than the covenant it implements.
The acknowledgment "that damages are not adequate" is in tension with Section 9.2 of the Lease, which gives Tenant both damages and injunctive relief for breach of the same restrictions.

The recital equates the leased "Premises" with the whole "Property", while Exhibit F, Section 1 describes the Premises as located "on the portion of the property" legally described, leaving the two descriptions of the demised area inconsistent.

Subordination "in all respects" to the Mortgage sits against Section 2 of the same agreement, which promises nondisturbance and provides that conflicts between the Lease and the Mortgage "shall be resolved in favor of the Lease".

The promise that any Lease/Mortgage conflict is "resolved in favor of the Lease" is difficult to reconcile with Section 1, under which the Lease is subordinate to the Mortgage "in all respects", and with Section 3(d)'s limits on Lender's liability.

Clause (d)(ii) frees Lender from claims, defenses and offsets arising before it takes possession, yet the same clause preserves "any rights of self-help, set-off, abatement or termination expressly provided in the Lease", leaving the two provisos pulling against each other.

The clause overrides the Lease "[n]otwithstanding any provisions of the Lease to the contrary", which cannot be squared with Section 25.3 of the Lease, providing that in any conflict between the Lease and an exhibit "the terms of this Lease will prevail".

Lender may impose its own "reasonable and customary procedures" for disbursing proceeds, which has to be reconciled with Section 15.2 of the Lease requiring an escrow "mutually satisfactory to Landlord and Tenant".
The "absolute right ... without Landlord's or Lender's further approval" is contradicted within the same section by the closing proviso that documents be "in a form acceptable to Lender".

An entire-agreement clause superseding "all prior or contemporaneous written or oral agreements" is hard to square with the Lease it is attached to and with Section 8, which states the agreement "shall not modify or in any way affect Landlord's obligations under the Lease".

The legal description carries the same incomplete call as the Lease's Exhibit A ("intersection with the division on the west and the property now or formerly owned by said Louis Tokos"), leaving one boundary line unrunnable.

The Memorandum places the Premises "on the portion of the property legally described on Exhibit A", while the Lease Recitals define the Premises as the Building, other improvements and the whole Land.

The recorded term "expiring on the fifteenth (15th) anniversary date of the Commencement Date" conflicts with Section 2.2 of the Lease (last day of the fifteenth Lease Year, subject to the Section 3.3 extension to January 31).
This copy of the legal description repeats the defective call at "its intersection with the division on the west", so the recorded description of the property does not close on its own terms.
